-The built-in guards cover checks that most applications share — personal data, topics, prompt injection. When you need something specific to your product, **fine-tune your own model**: give Opik a labeled dataset and a description of what to catch, and it trains a language model into a check that answers one yes-or-no question about a piece of text, such as "does this reply read as off-brand?" or "is this abusive?".

+The built-in rules cover checks that most applications share — personal data, topics, prompt injection. When you need something specific to your product, **fine-tune your own model**: give Opik a labeled dataset and a description of what to catch, and it trains a language model into a check that answers one yes-or-no question about a piece of text, such as "does this reply read as off-brand?" or "is this abusive?".

Opik runs the whole loop for you. There is no training infrastructure to set up and nothing to deploy: you supply the examples, Opik fine-tunes the model on its GPUs, reports how accurate it turned out, and serves it inline from that point on. You can do it [from the UI](#create-a-model-in-the-ui) or [from the SDK](#fine-tune-from-the-sdk).

+### Upgrading from guards

+Earlier SDK versions called rules _guards_ and ran PII, Topic, and prompt injection on the guardrails server with a threshold you set. Opik now checks them itself and sets the thresholds, so code written for the older API needs these changes:
+| Before | Now |
+| `Guardrail(guards=[...])` | `Guardrail(rules=[...])` |
+| `from opik.guardrails.guards import ...` | `from opik.guardrails import ...`, or `opik.guardrails.rules` |
+| `PII(blocked_entities=[...], threshold=..., language=...)` | `PII(entities=[...])` |

## What Opik offers
-- **Five guard types** — PII detection, allowed and restricted topics, prompt injection and jailbreak detection, an LLM-as-a-judge check written in plain language, and your own trained classifier.
+- **Five rule types** — PII detection, allowed and restricted topics, prompt injection and jailbreak detection, an LLM-as-a-judge check written in plain language, and your own trained classifier.

- **Stored policies** — define your checks once in the Opik UI and reference them by name from your application. Workspace-wide policies can also be enforced on every application, whether or not it asks for them.

-- **Model fine-tuning** — for a check the built-in guards do not cover, fine-tune a language model on your own labeled examples. Opik hosts the training, reports how accurate the result is, and serves the model inline. No training infrastructure of your own, and no deployment step.

+- **Model fine-tuning** — for a check the built-in rules do not cover, fine-tune a language model on your own labeled examples. Opik hosts the training, reports how accurate the result is, and serves the model inline. No training infrastructure of your own, and no deployment step.
- **Full observability** — every guardrail run is logged as a span on the trace it protects, so you can inspect what failed and track failure rates over time.

-| **Policy** | A named group of guards, stored in your workspace. Your application references the name, so the checks can change without a code change. |

+| **Policy** | A named group of rules, stored in your workspace. Your application references the name, so the checks can change without a code change. |
+| **Guardrail** | What your application actually calls. You build it from one or more policies, rules defined in code, or both, and it runs every rule they hold on each piece of text you give it. |
